1.q: After these things and these acts of faithfulness
1.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **faithfulness**, you can express the same idea with a verbal form such as “faithfully.” Alternate translation: [After Hezekiah faithfully did all the things Yahweh commanded him to do]

1.q: Sennacherib, king of Assyria, came … He camped
1.note: Here Sennacherib represents his army. Alternate translation: [Sennacherib, king of Assyria, and his army came … They camped]
Here “came” can be stated as “went.” Alternate translation: [went and entered Judah]

2.q: that Sennacherib had come and that he intended
2.note: Here Sennacherib also represents his army. Alternate translation: [that Sennacherib and his army had come and that they intended]
Here “Jerusalem” represents the people there. Alternate translation: [to fight against the people of Jerusalem] or [to fight against the army of Jerusalem]

3.q: to stop up the waters of the springs that were outside the city
3.note: The people of the city would fill up wells and fountain springs with earth and rocks, hiding the water from the Assyrians, but the people would cause the water to flow into the city through secret pathways.

4.q: Why should the kings of Assyria come and find a lot of water?
4.note: The people use a rhetorical question to emphasize that they do not want the kings of Assyria to find their water. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [We do not want the kings of Assyria to come here and find a lot of water.]

Here, the word **kings** could mean: (1) this is an idiom that refers to the one king of Assyria. Alternate translation: [the king of Assyria] or (2) this may refer to the king and his other leaders. Alternate translation: [the king and the other leaders of Assyria]

5.q: Hezekiah took courage and built up … He built … He also … he made
5.note: The readers should understand that Hezekiah probably commanded other people to do the actual work. Alternate translation: [Hezekiah took courage and commanded the people to build up … They built … They also … they made]

5.q: Hezekiah took courage and built up
5.note: This could mean: (1) Hezekiah strengthened his position by commanding the people to repair the walls of the city. You can make this clear by using the connecting word “by.” Alternate translation: [Hezekiah strengthened the city by building up] or (2) he became encouraged. Alternate translation: [Hezekiah became encouraged and built up]
This is a part of the wall on the north side of Jerusalem.

6.q: He placed military commanders over the people
6.note: The idiom “place over” means to put in charge of. “He put military commanders in charge of the people”

7.q: for someone is with us who is greater than those with him
7.note: Alternate translation: [for our God is with us and is more powerful than those with the king of Assyria]

8.q: is only an arm of flesh
8.note: Here “arm” represents strength, and “flesh” represents humanity. Alternate translation: [are only those with human power]

9.note: The word “now” is used here to mark a break in the main story line. Here the narrator tells background information about the location of Sennacherib and his army.
This was a city in Judah.

10.q: What are you relying on in order to endure a siege in Jerusalem?
10.note: Sennacherib uses a rhetorical question to cause the people to think about their situation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [You are not able to endure a siege in Jerusalem.]

11.q: Is not Hezekiah misleading you … king of Assyria’?
11.note: Sennacherib uses a rhetorical question to cause the people of Jerusalem to think about their situation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [Hezekiah is misleading you … king of Assyria.’]

11.q: that he may give you over to die by famine and by thirst
11.note: Alternate translation: [so that you will die from lack of food and water]

11.q: from the hand of the king of Assyria
11.note: Here “hand” represents power or control. Alternate translation: [from the power of the king of Assyria] or [from the king of Assyria]

12.q: Has not this same Hezekiah taken away … sacrifices’?
12.note: Sennacherib uses a rhetorical question to cause the people of Jerusalem to think about their situation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [This is the same Hezekiah who has taken away … sacrifices.’] or [Hezekiah has taken away … sacrifices.’]
Here “Judah” and “Jerusalem” represent the people who live there. Alternate translation: [commanded the people of Judah and Jerusalem]

13.q: Do you not know what … lands?
13.note: Sennacherib uses a rhetorical question to cause the people of Jerusalem to think about their situation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [You know very well what … lands!]

Sennacherib uses a rhetorical question to cause the people of Jerusalem to think about their situation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [There was no god … power!]

14.q: Among all the gods … was there any god who … hand?
14.note: Sennacherib uses a rhetorical question to cause the people of Jerusalem to think about their situation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [There was no god among all the gods … who … hand!]
Here “hand” represents power or control. Alternate translation: [from my power] or [from me]

14.q: Why should your God be able … power?
14.note: Sennacherib uses a rhetorical question to cause the people of Jerusalem to think about their situation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [There is no reason your God should be able … power!]

15.note: Here the word “now” is used to draw attention to the important point that follows.

15.q: How much less will your God rescue you from my hand?
15.note: Sennacherib uses a rhetorical question to cause the people of Jerusalem to think about their situation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [Your God will certainly not be able to rescue you from my hand!]

17.note: Here “hand” represents power or control. Alternate translation: [from my power] or [from me]

18.q: to frighten them and trouble them
18.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing and emphasize the intensity of fear. Alternate translation: [to make them very afraid]
Alternate translation: [the Assyrian army might capture]

19.q: They spoke of the God of Jerusalem as they had spoken of the gods of the other peoples of the earth
19.note: Alternate translation: [They mocked the God of Jerusalem as they had mocked the gods of the other peoples of the earth]

19.q: which are merely the work of men’s hands
19.note: This emphasizes that humans made these idols with their own hands and are therefore worthless. Alternate translation: [which are merely idols that men have made]

20.note: Here “heaven” represents Yahweh. Alternate translation: [cried to Yahweh for help] or [pleaded to Yahweh]

21.note: Alternate translation: [the temple of his god]

22.q: from the hand of Sennacherib … from the hand of all others
22.note: Here “hand” represents power or control. Alternate translation: [from the power of Sennacherib … from the power of all others] or [from Sennacherib … from all others]

22.q: gave them rest on every side
22.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **rest**, you can express the same idea with a verbal form such as “peacefully.” Alternate translation: [caused them to live peacefully with all the people of the nations around them]

23.q: he was lifted up in the eyes of all nations
23.note: Here “lifted up” is an idiom that means to honor. Also, “in the eyes” is a metaphor that represents judgment or evaluation. Alternate translation: [the people of all the nations honored him] (See also: [Metaphor](ta:figs-metaphor))

24.note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that he would heal Hezekiah]

25.q: But Hezekiah did not pay back Yahweh for the help given to him
25.note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But Hezekiah did not act in a grateful way after Yahweh helped him]

Here “heart” is a metonym that represents a person’s inner being. Here “heart was lifted up” is an idiom that means to become proud. Alternate translation: [he became proud] (See also: [Idiom](ta:figs-idiom))

25.q: So anger came on him, and on Judah and Jerusalem
25.note: Yahweh becoming angry and punishing the people is spoken of as if “anger came on” them. “Judah” and “Jerusalem” are metonyms that represent the people who live there. Alternate translation: [So Yahweh became angry and punished him and the people of Judah and Jerusalem] (See also: [Metonymy](ta:figs-metonymy))

26.note: Alternate translation: [during Hezekiah’s lifetime] or [during Hezekiah’s reign as king]

28.note: This is a small enclosure where horses are kept. See how you translated this in 2 Chronicles 9:25
a storage place for small animals

30.q: Hezekiah who also stopped up … and who brought them straight down
30.note: The readers should understand that Hezekiah probably commanded other people to do the actual work. Alternate translation: [Hezekiah who ordered his workers to stop up … and to build a tunnel so that the water would flow down]
This is the name of a stream near Jerusalem.

31.q: the miraculous sign that had been done in the land
31.note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the miracle that Yahweh had performed in the land]

31.q: to know all that was in his heart
31.note: Here “heart” represents a person’s inner being. Alternate translation: [to reveal Hezekiah’s true character]

33.note: This was a polite way to tell about him dying. See how you translated this in 2 Chronicles 9:31. Alternate translation: [Hezekiah died]
